description: We are engineering students in computer science, software engineering, and cybersecurity. We love tackling technical challenges, writing clean code, and building secure systems. Passionate about astronomy and space tech.
summary:
Planetary Analog Finder is an open, interactive map that searches all of Earth's barren land
for the best places to prepare for the Moon and Mars. Instead of starting from a few
famous analog sites, it compares every 0.25° tile with two targets, Jezero Crater on Mars
and the lunar south pole, dimension by dimension and in physical units: day–night
temperature swing, night temperature, albedo, slope, roughness, rock type, dryness and
sun angle. Three mission profiles (rover navigation, geology, polar operations) turn these
into ranked, explained shortlists, and clustering reveals "hidden gems": high-scoring sites
in the same terrain family as known analogs that nobody uses yet. We validated the method on real test sites: for rover navigation, Atacama, Mojave and Haughton Crater
rank in the top 7% of Earth's barren land. Every site card also says where the analogy
breaks, from gravity to radiation, so teams know what Earth can and cannot reproduce.
details:
- What it does: the summary's method, then the user flow: pick a target and a mission,

click a site, read its score, radar, "works for" and "breaks"; Top sites, Hidden gems and

Validation tabs; Orbi answers questions about the data.

- How it works: Python pipeline on Google Earth Engine with NASA and ESA data → per-

dimension closeness scores → weighted totals → K-Means clustering → validation

against known analogs → static website (HTML, JavaScript,

Leaflet, Chart.js) on GitHub Pages; Orbi's open questions go to an open AI model

(Llama 4 Scout) through a Cloudflare Worker.

- Benefits and impact: cheaper, closer test sites for rover, instrument and procedure

tests; a transparent list of what each site can and cannot reproduce; an open tool any

team can reuse and extend.

- What we found: validation results, the 2–3 hidden gems, the polar failure and why.

- Creativity: systematic search instead of known sites; validation built in; honest "where

it breaks" on every card; an assistant that explains the data.

- Factors we considered: scale (0.25° tiles, re-scoring at 30 m as next step), missing

data (dust, gaps in rock type), Earth's unchangeable differences (gravity,

atmosphere, radiation), honest validation rules.

- Links: repo https://github.com/Dragonsvil/NASA-Space-Challenge-2026.
